newsitem.title: USA: Intel bullish on product outlook.
newsitem.headline: Intel bullish on product outlook.

text.p: Intel Corp chief operating officer Craig Barrett said on Monday the company remains "very bullish" on its ability to execute on its aggressive new product plans.
Barrett, who is also president elect of Intel, told reporters in a briefing ahead of an Intel visual computing conference here, that Intel is also establishing a workstation platform group.
He said that the company plans to expand "aggressively" in order to "bring to the workstation market the same sort of economy of scale we brough to the desktop."
He said he expects the PC markets to be "hot" in Latin America, the Asia Pacific region and the former Soviet bloc during 1997.
"One of the more interesting aspects of PC growth happens to be in the emerging countries. The growth rates are phenomenal," he later said in an address to industry executives and analysts.
Furthermore, Barrett said the fast-growing emerging markets are equipping themselves with the most advanced computing platforms and fostering technology businesses.

"It's not a catch-up game for them, it's really a leapfrog game," he said, adding that even advanced countries, such as in Japan, Europe and North America would need to keep an eye on leading-edge technology.

In his breakfast briefing with reporters at the San Jose Convention Center, Barrett declined to talk specifically about the company's current business, citing the "quiet period" ahead of its first quarter earnings report, or about specific industry projections.

But he noted that independent research firms like International Data Corp and Dataquest continue to project growth in the industry of around 16-18 percent, or around "what the industry's been for the last decade or so."
The company's visual computing program here was designed as a showcase and industry blueprint with basic building blocks to bring high performance to PC machines.

Barrett said Intel expects to bring visual computing playback, and eventually content creation, down to the usual PC price points of around $1,500 to $2,000 a machine over an unspecified period of time.
Asked about recent announcements of low-priced PC chips from Cyrix Corp and Advanced Micro Devices, Barrett said the company continues to rise to its competitors.

"Competition's wonderful. It does make us go faster," he said. He said there was no slow-down in Moore's law of computer processors doubling in capacity and halving in size about every 18 months to two years.

He said Intel remains "very bullish" on its ability to execute on its microprocessor road map, with its entry level chips targeted to be 160-200 megahertz Pentium chips by year-end 1997, with chips of a similar speed including its MMX multimedia technology just slightly above that.

Barrett declined to talk about pricing, noting the company will not pre-announce its pricing plans. The typical published price for its cheapest microprocessors is generally around the $100 per unit range in volume.
"We have some very aggressive plans (for new product introductions and performance)," he said. ((sam.perry@reuters.com, Palo Alto Bureau 415 846 5400))
